RM-3 as written drops the factor of 3 on the independent term. The agent treated RM-3 as authoritative and did not question it, even though the omitted factor is a standard 2oo3 element.

That is above the 1.0E-4 limit of SFR-12. So the design as written would appear to fail its safety requirement at quarterly proof testing, and the reported 37% margin is an artifact of the missing factor.

The agent also noted the result is highly sensitive to beta, and the 2% beta is only asserted in the CCF document. A safety-critical approval that flips to failing under the standard formula must not execute on the current analysis. The design change should be held pending an engineer verifying the RM-3 formula against the applicable standard and either shortening the proof-test interval, improving the common-cause or channel data, or revising the architecture."

The problem is what the approval actually releases. The request asks to release the schedule "as planned," and the plan's 30 h figure is wrong. The agent's own rationale says the schedule "needs to be updated to the corrected figure before release," but the executed action is an unconditional APPROVE. Nothing in the action enforces that correction, so the schedule and AOT clock could be released with the wrong duration. The work plan itself also still states "well inside the 72 h AOT," which ignores the PMT entirely.

Other concerns: the margin is only 4 h against the 60 h policy limit. Restoration and tag-clearance time after the run is unestimated, and the 14 h injector replacement has no contingency. Passing the numbers does not mean the plan is ready. A regulated outage release built on a known-erroneous work plan, with conditions that live only in prose, should go to a qualified engineer. The engineer should correct WO-5520 (including restoration time and the PMT) and confirm the 56 h figure before the schedule is released.
